pages.name: The hinge
pages.text: Two straight arms are joined at a hinge. Arm `a` is 3 long, arm `b` is 4 long, and `C` is the angle between them. The third side, `c`, joins their free ends. Each side takes the small letter of the corner opposite it. At 90° Pythagoras gives `c² = 9 + 16 = 25`, so `c = 5`. Close the hinge and the free ends come together, so `c` is shorter. Open it and they move apart, so `c` is longer. Drag the end of arm `a`.

pages.name: c at 120°
pages.task: The hinge opens to 120°. How long is `c` now?
pages.why: Past 90° the free ends are further apart than at a right angle, so `c` is longer than Pythagoras' 5. The bars show by how much. The correction adds 12, so `c² = 25 + 12 = 37` and `c = 6.08`.

pages.name: Building the rule
pages.text: Where does the correction come from? Lay arm `b` along the across axis from the hinge, so its free end is at `(b, 0)`. Arm `a` is lesson 3's turning arm made `a` times longer, so its tip is at `(a cos C, a sin C)`. The gap between the free ends is `b − a cos C` across and `a sin C` up, so Pythagoras on that gap gives `c²`. Multiply it out, and lesson 3's `cos² C + sin² C = 1` turns the last two terms into `a²`. Drag the end of arm `a`.

pages.name: c² at 60°
pages.task: The hinge closes to 60°, where `cos 60° = 0.5`. What is `c²`?
pages.why: Here `a² + b² = 25` and `2ab = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24`. So `c² = 25 − 24 × 0.5 = 25 − 12 = 13`, multiplying before taking away. That makes `c = 3.61`, shorter than Pythagoras' 5.

pages.name: Flat and folded
pages.text: Past 90° the tip of arm `a` swings left of the hinge, so `cos C` turns negative. At 110°, `cos 110° = −0.342`. The correction takes away `24 × cos C`, and taking away a negative adds, so its bar stands above the line and `c` is longer than Pythagoras gives. Laid flat at 180°, the arms make one straight line and `c = 3 + 4 = 7`. Folded shut at 0°, they lie together and `c = 4 − 3 = 1`. Drag the end of arm `a`.

pages.task: The hinge opens to 110°, where `cos 110° = −0.342`. How long is `c`?
pages.why: `c² = 25 − 24 × (−0.342)`. Taking away a negative adds, so `c² = 25 + 8.21 = 33.21` and `c = 5.76`. That is longer than Pythagoras' 5, because the hinge is past 90°.

pages.name: Back to the angle
pages.text: The rule also runs backwards, from three sides to an angle. Rearrange it to `cos C = (a² + b² − c²) ÷ 2ab`, with `c` the side opposite the angle you want, and press `cos⁻¹`. With arms 3 and 4 and a third side of 6, `cos C = (9 + 16 − 36) ÷ 24 = −0.458`, so `C = 117.3°`. Each angle from 0° to 180° has a cosine of its own, so `cos⁻¹` gives the one angle that fits, acute or obtuse.

pages.name: Sides 5, 8 and 7
pages.task: A triangle has sides 5, 8 and 7. What is the angle `C`, opposite the side of 7?

pages.name: A height, twice
pages.text: Now a second rule. In a triangle `ABC`, drop a line from `B` square onto side `AC`. It makes two right-angled triangles, and lesson 1's sine gives the height, `h`, twice. In the left one `h = c sin A`, and in the right one `h = a sin C`. So `c sin A = a sin C`, and dividing both sides by `sin A sin C` gives `a ÷ sin A = c ÷ sin C`. If `A` is past 90°, the height lands outside, beyond `A`, but lesson 3's `sin (180° − A) = sin A` keeps the rule the same. A height from another corner brings in `b` the same way.

pages.name: Side b
pages.task: In triangle `ABC`, `A = 40°`, `B = 60°` and `a = 5`. How long is `b`?

pages.name: The swing arm
pages.text: Finding an angle with the sine rule has a catch. Here side `b = 8` rises at 30° from corner `A` to corner `C`, 4 above the base line. From `C` an arm `a` swings round, and wherever its end meets the base line is a corner `B`. An arm of 3 falls short. At 5 it lands twice, since `sin B = 8 × 0.5 ÷ 5 = 0.8` gives `B = 53.1°`, and `180° − 53.1° = 126.9°` shares that sine. At 8 or longer the second landing is at `A` or behind it, so one triangle is left. Drag the knob along the scale for arm `a`.

pages.name: Two ships
pages.task: Two ships sail from one port, 48 and 40 nautical miles, on courses 113° apart. How far apart are they, in nautical miles?
pages.why: Two sides and the angle between them call for the cosine rule. Here `48² + 40² = 3904`, `2 × 48 × 40 = 3840` and `cos 113° = −0.390731`, which is negative, so the correction adds: `d² = 3904 − 3840 × (−0.390731) = 3904 + 1500.41 = 5404.41`, and `d = 73.5`.

pages.name: A right angle
pages.task: This triangle has a right angle between its sides of 5 and 2. Which finds the angle `θ`, opposite the 2, in one step?
pages.why: There is a right angle, so lesson 1's ratios are all you need. The 2 is opposite `θ` and the 5 is next to it, so `tan θ = 2 ÷ 5 = 0.4` and `θ = tan⁻¹ 0.4 = 21.8°`. The cosine rule would get there only after finding the third side, and the sine rule needs a known side facing a known angle, which this triangle does not have.

pages.name: The engine, a stretch
pages.task: A stretch, with example figures. In an engine, the crankshaft centre, the crankpin and the piston pin make a triangle. Say the crank is 50 mm, the connecting rod 200 mm, and the crank is turned 40° from the cylinder's centre line. What is the rod's angle `θ` to the centre line?
pages.why: Pair each side with the angle opposite it. The rod, 200, faces the 40°, and the crank, 50, faces `θ`. So `sin θ = 50 × sin 40° ÷ 200 = 0.161`, and `sin⁻¹` gives 9.2°. `180° − 9.2° = 170.8°` shares the sine, but `170.8° + 40°` is over 180°, so only 9.2° fits.
